title: Iran faces 'greatest financial offensive ever', says US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent
description: The US announced a host of sanctions against Iran and threatened its supporters in what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said was "the single greatest
body: The US announced a host of sanctions against Iran and threatened its supporters in what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said was "the single greatest financial offensive ever".Labelling it an "economic D-Day" for Iran, Bessent said the US would sever all economic ties with the country and added that any nation financially partnering with Iran would also be isolated. However, the latest threat to the Iranian regime follows several U-turns and extended deadlines from the White House in its efforts to end the conflict.In response, Iran's economy minister Ali Madanizadeh said there was a two-year plan to counter the sanctions, which would result in another defeat for Washington.The war has led to hikes in global oil prices, and in response to the latest threat Iran warned it would shut down all oil exports from the region if the war continuedThe Iranian regime has also issued a fresh warning to shipping to not pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its permission, according to Reuters.One fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes through the strait, a narrow waterway south of Iran, but the flow has been effectively blocked by the country since the conflict began at the end of February, leading to higher oil prices globally.At a press conference on Monday outlining what has been called "Operation Economic Outcast", Bessent said the US was launching an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe"."Iran now faces a very clear choice with only two paths before them: complete global isolation....or a path back to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy," he said.The treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it".Bessent said the Treasury Department had mapped networks, facilitators and financial channels used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil.The department said it had issued determinations against five sectors: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. The Treasury has also imposed sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels.Bessent said that such actions would "tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue" for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the wider Iranian regime. In a warning to governments and entities assisting or trading with Iran, he said they could not "claim they are blind to enabling this activity".He declined to highlight specific countries, but said Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime".While he said it was important to give people time to understand the new sanctions, he added: "They should know that we will move very quickly and that we are serious."Madanizadeh said Iran was "fully prepared for the US sanctions"."We've been waiting for these plans for a long time, and the government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television.He also said neither China nor Russia had "accepted" the US measures, and predicted other countries would resist them.The Chinese Foreign Ministry said sanctions and pressure tactics did not help and Beijing would do what was necessary to protect China's interests.David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, cast doubt on the effectiveness of the sanctions announcement."With the renewed US naval blockade already strangling Iran's oil exports, the direct impact of 'economic D-Day' on Iran's energy revenues will be somewhat of a damp squib," he said."We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term."He said that was partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, a country "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either".Over the course of the conflict so far, previous threats have included Trump saying in April that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" unless Iran agreed a deal to end the war and unblock the Strait of Hormuz.The US eventually climbed down from that position after mediator Pakistan intervened and called for more diplomacy.The economic impact of the Iran war is being felt in the US and across the world. Higher oil prices have fuelled concerns over the cost of living, with petrol and diesel  prices much higher than they were a year ago. In the US, gasoline prices have surpassed $4 a gallon and affordability is among the top concerns of American voters ahead of the mid-term elections in November.On Monday, a barrel of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, was $92.Last week, Bessent announced the US government would intervene in the bond markets and buy back more government debt in a bid to boost demand for bonds and lower borrowing rates.But the impact of the announcenment was short-lived, with long-term borrowing costs bouncing back up a day later.

schema.headline: Iran faces 'greatest financial offensive ever', says US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent

title: Kit Harington joins HBO's Harry Potter series as Gilderoy Lockhart
description: Kit Harington has been tapped to join the highly anticipated Harry Potter TV series as the wizarding world's celebrity-turned-Hogwarts instructor Gild
body: Kit Harington has been tapped to join the highly anticipated Harry Potter TV series as the wizarding world's celebrity-turned-Hogwarts instructor Gilderoy Lockhart, HBO confirmed to the BBC.Harington is replacing actor Nicholas Hoult who could not film season two of the series due to a scheduling conflict.Best known for playing Jon Snow for eight seasons in the award-winning series Game of Thrones, Harington also appears in the BBC and HBO financial drama Industry. The casting marks the English actor's third collaboration with the American network and streamer.Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone is due to premiere on Christmas this year on HBO Max. Season two will adapt the second book in the series by JK Rowling, The Chamber of Secrets, which chronicle's Potter's second year at the magical school. "Before we begin year two at Hogwarts, there has been a slight change due to schedule: Kit Harington will be stepping into the role of Gilderoy Lockhart," a story post reads on the official Harry Potter Instagram account. The new series adaptation of the best-selling books stars newcomer Dominic McLaughlin as the boy wizard, Alastair Stout as his best friend Ron Weasley and Arabella Stanton as the young witch Hermione Granger. Oscar-nominated actor Jon Lithgow has been cast as Hogwarts headmaster Albus Dumbledore and Nick Frost as gamekeeper Rubeus Hagrid.Emmy-award winning Harington, a lifelong fan of the books, already has some familiarity with his new role: The actor voiced Lockhart in Audible's star-studded Harry Potter: The Full-Cast Audio Editions last year.The show could reunite him with director and producer Mark Mylod, who worked on Game of Thrones and is directing some Harry Potter episodes. Mylod is an executive producer on the new series along with author JK Rowling.Lockhart was portrayed in the Warner Bros Harry Potter films by Kenneth Branagh, and is a key character in Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets, the second book in Rowling's best-selling franchise.The vain wizard who authored several books on his purported encounters with dark creatures serves as Hogwarts' latest professor for the defence against the dark arts and fancies himself a mentor to Harry in his second year.Hoult, known for his roles in X-Men, Superman and Mad Max: Fury Road, was announced for the role earlier this month. But HBO reportedly had to let the Superman actor out of his deal due to his commitments to projects that conflicted with a change in the series' production schedule, according to Deadline, which first reported Harington's casting. HBO confirmed the reporting to the BBC. Representatives for Harington and Hoult did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The HBO series is expected to take 10 years to complete, as producers plan multiple seasons covering each of Rowling's seven books, which the eight blockbuster films were originally based on.

schema.headline: Kit Harington joins HBO's Harry Potter series as Gilderoy Lockhart

title: Prince Harry steps down from African Parks charity board
description: The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses a
body: The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses against indigenous people.A spokesman for Prince Harry confirmed he was stepping down after being president for the charity, African Parks, for six years before becoming a member of its board of directors in 2023, but said he remains a "supporter of its mission".Last year the organisation admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.Prince Harry's resignation comes shortly after it was announced he was relocating with the Duchess of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet from California to the UK.Prince Harry's spokesman said "the Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board."His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks' mission."African Parks manages around 20 national parks and protected areas across 12 countries.It was subject to an independent human rights investigation into allegations guards managed and paid by the charity had beaten, raped and tortured indigenous people in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park.The charity said in 2025 it had improved its safeguarding processes both in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park and institutionally. Announcing a "governance refresh of its board of directors", the charity thanked Prince Harry for his association, saying he had "brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa".It added: "The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks' work."The charity's website says Prince Harry served as part of the expert team that helped implement the first phase of the 500 Elephants project, which was "one of the largest and most significant elephant translocations in conservation history".It saw wildlife experts move elephants from a park in Malawi to help increase population in areas where they have been heavily poached.Prince Harry has said helping move elephants to safer homes was an "amazing" experience.The Sussexes are back in the spotlight after the revelation last week they were returning to the UK this month after enrolling their children to start at a British school in September.No change is expected to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.Their pending return to the UK has raised questions on their security arrangements.Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.The couple's plans while they are in the UK are also unclear. The BBC learned the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, which would be her first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.In early 2020, the Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties before settling in California in March that year.

schema.headline: Prince Harry steps down from African Parks charity board

title: Sir Chris Hoy: Campaigning for cancer screening should not be down to me
description: Figure caption, Chris Hoy says men must understand their prostate cancer riskByJane LewisBBC Sport Scotland Senior ReporterSir Chris Hoy believes the
body: Figure caption, Chris Hoy says men must understand their prostate cancer riskByJane LewisBBC Sport Scotland Senior ReporterSir Chris Hoy believes the onus to encourage men to get tested for prostate cancer should not just be on high-profile individuals like him.Hoy told BBC Scotland he felt privileged to have the public platform to spread awareness and would continue to do so even if there was a national screening system in place.But he said: "It shouldn't just be down to high-profile individuals like Jeremy Clarkson or myself or any number of men who've been in a similar situation. "There should be a more systematic and proactive approach to let men know about their own risk."Sir Chris was diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer when was 47.. He turned 50 in March.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Hoy uses his profile as a well-known and well-loved public figure to campaign for prostate screeningHe told BBC Scotland: "I turned 50 recently and I got a letter through the post with a bowel screening test."I understand the PSA test (a blood test that can help detect prostate cancer) isn't perfect, you know you can get results - not false positives, but it can be that men can be treated when they maybe didn't need to be treated."But actually, I think that's not a diagnosis issue, that's a treatment issue, that's a decision for the doctors to make."I think knowing your situation is really important."Hoy said 10,000 men a year in the UK find out too late that they have prostate cancer.He said there should be some kind of formal process to at least make men take responsibility and ownership and to understand their personal risk."In the short term, until something more proactive happens you've got to take it on your own shoulders," he said."It's not what you want to think about and it's always the thing you push down the list of priorities. You forget about it because life's busy."Image source, Scottish PowerImage caption, Sir Chris Hoy meets employees from Tour de 4 backer ScottishPower for a special training session at Bellahouston Park, Glasgow.The six-time Olympic gold medallist, was speaking ahead of his "'Tour De 4" charity cycle, the event he founded after his diagnosis which, in his view, is "doing something positive from a very difficult situation.""The aim is to try and change perceptions of what living with stage 4 cancer can mean," he said.As well as raising money, he said the event aimed to "bring together people who are in a similar situation to me, to bring together families, people who are remembering loved ones"."It's really a celebration of life," he said.While Sir Chris is an ardent campaigner for prostate cancer, he admits to being "moved" by Scottish swimmer Archie Goodburn's impassioned plea to the prime minister for increased funding for brain cancer, and hopes something will come of it."So far, it seems that the powers-that-be are listening," he said.'I'm not going to give up'"My concern is that you get a lot of publicity from something like that and then the politicians, or the people in power or whoever the decision-makers are, will do something as a reaction - 'oh yes we're going to have a chat' or 'we're going to do this', but actions speak louder than words."You want to see some practical change that will actually be implemented, not just a sit-down-and-talk and 'we might address this' and 'we'll have a look at it' because often that means 'we're just going to kick the can down the road' and nothing actually changes.""But Archie's not going to give up and I'm not going to give up."Sir Chris said he was "doing really well" at the moment.He added: "Right now life just goes on. You could spent your time sitting worrying about the future but that doesn't help you in any shape or form."The Tour De 4 takes place on Sunday 6 September, starting and finishing at the Sir Chris Hoy velodrome in Glasgow.

schema.headline: Sir Chris Hoy: Campaigning for cancer screening should not be down to me

title: Lockerbie bombing trial postponed days before it was due to start
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Pan Am Flight 103 was brought down on 21 December 1988ByScotland home affairs correspondentThe trial of a Libyan m
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Pan Am Flight 103 was brought down on 21 December 1988ByScotland home affairs correspondentThe trial of a Libyan man over the Lockerbie bombing has been postponed for a third time, after new evidence on the 37-year-old case came to light three days ago.Jury selection was due to get under way in Washington DC on Wednesday but the BBC understands a new start date has been set for January next year.Lawyers acting for Abu Agila Mohammad Kheir Al-Marimi said "newly discovered evidence" previously unknown to the defence and prosecutors from the US government emerged on Friday 21 August.Al-Marimi has denied building the bomb that destroyed Pan Am Flight 103 on December 21, 1988, killing 270 people.His lawyers told the court: "Constitutional and ethical obligations require the defence to investigate this development."They said they met Al-Marimi on Sunday and he agreed that they should ask for the postponement.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi has been in custody since December 2022The trial judge, Dabney Friedrich, has agreed that the start date should be set aside, underlining the potential importance of the new evidence.She would have been extremely reluctant to allow an 11th hour postponement after months of preparation and marathon pre-trial legal battles.For the relatives of those who died and Al-Marimi himself, this latest delay means a verdict might not come until next spring.It is yet another stunning development in a saga that has witnessed countless twists and turns over nearly four decades.Pan Am 103 was flying from Heathrow to New York when the bomb exploded in its forward hold, breaking the plane apart at 31,000 feet.All 259 passengers and crew on board were killed.  Another 11 people died in Lockerbie when the wreckage fell on their homes.Of the victims, 190 were American and 43 from the UK.Nearly four decades later, the bombing remains the worst terror attack and mass murder in British history.'Disappointing for the families'Al-Marimi has been in US custody since 2022 and was originally due to stand trial in May 2025.That date was set aside following a joint request from the prosecution and defence, who cited the complexity of the case and Al-Marimi's ill health.The trial was pencilled in for April this year but was called off again, after the defence asked for more time to prepare.The Lockerbie bombing has been the subject of a joint Scottish-US investigation since December 1988.Prosecutors from the Crown Office and detectives from Police Scotland were due to travel to Washington to attend the case, and Scottish witnesses were expected to be among the first to give evidence at the trial.Laura Buchan, head of the Lockerbie investigation team at the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service said:  "I recognise that this adjournment will be disappointing for the families and for those who have followed this case over many years."As the matter remains before the court, it would not be appropriate to comment on the reasons for the adjournment. Although these proceedings are being led by the United States authorities, Scottish prosecutors and police officers remain fully committed to supporting the pursuit of justice."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was the only man convicted of the Lockerbie bombingA grandfather in his 70s, Al-Marimi has been accused of carrying out the attack along with two Libyans who faced a Scottish court in May 2000.Three judges heard the case at Camp Zeist, a former US air force base in the Netherlands.After eight months, they ruled the atrocity was an act of state sponsored terrorism carried out by members of the Libyan intelligence service.The judges convicted one of the Libyans, Abdulbasset Al-Megrahi, of mass murder and jailed him for life.He died from cancer in 2012, after being freed on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government.The Scottish Criminal Cases Review Conviction twice referred Megrahi's case to the appeal court but the conviction was upheld.The second Libyan, Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah was acquitted and returned home to a hero's welcome in Tripoli.The US government says Al-Marimi admitted bombing the plane along with Megrahi and Fhimah when he was questioned in a Libyan detention facility in 2012.The alleged confession was handed to Scottish investigators in 2017 and is now central to the prosecution case.Al-Marimi has claimed the confession is false and was made under duress, but judge Friedrich ruled it can be admitted as evidence at the trial.

schema.headline: Lockerbie bombing trial postponed days before it was due to start

title: Why some US restaurants are banning tips
description: 'What you see is what you pay' - why some US restaurants are banning tipsImage source, Caroline KraetzerImage caption, Caroline Kraetzer no longer get
body: 'What you see is what you pay' - why some US restaurants are banning tipsImage source, Caroline KraetzerImage caption, Caroline Kraetzer no longer gets tips but her salary is double the normBySusie Bearne Wine waiter Caroline Kraetzer earns $40 (£30) an hour, double what most service staff in San Francisco are paid but then it costs a lot to eat at her restaurant.At a set price of $140 (£100) per person, La Cigale is one of a small number of restaurants charging higher prices so it can pay high salaries - and it doesn't allow tips.It tells customers: "What you see is what you pay. We do not accept tips, your kind words and return visits will suffice."Kraetzer says it is good to no longer be "reliant on the generosity of strangers to pay the bills".While waiting staff at other restaurants can make a lot of money from tips, she says "you're often there two hours before service, and again when you're closing after the guests have left, so you are making minimum wage during that time".Fairer for staff?On the other side of the US, Rachel Miller, chef and owner of Nightshade Noodle Bar in the town Lynn, Massachusetts, moved to a tip-free model five years ago when they reopened after the Covid-19 pandemic.Her motivation was to make it fairer for the kitchen staff. "The people breaking their backs and minds in the kitchen - often the least visible and the least celebrated - were taking home a fraction of what the front staff made on tips for the same hours," she says.Miller says she found it "deeply unsettling" to see higher tips going to white male staff and lower tips to everyone else. "Tipping lets guests, consciously or not, pay people differently based on gender, race, or sexuality and I was not willing to let that decide my team's income."To pay the staff higher wages, Miller also increased prices at the French-Vietnamese restaurant. Its tasting menus now start from £102 for seven courses before 6pm, and $126 for nine courses."Our prices are higher than a comparable restaurant's because they carry the full cost of paying people properly," says Miller. "That is the trade, and I stand behind it."Image source, Alyssa BlumsteinImage caption, Rachel Miller says that banning tips is fairer for her kitchen staffHow have customers reacted?Yet not every restaurant that has switched to a tipless model has made a success of it, as sometimes customers don't appreciate the higher menu prices.Talulla in Cambridge, Massachusetts, dropped tips in 2020 so it could pay staff more equitably, only to then switch back in September of last year."We tried to keep our non-tipping model simply by raising our menu prices 23%, but we were only able to sustain this through the winter months," says co-owner Danielle Ayer."Operating a non-tipped restaurant is more expensive overall," adds Ayer. This is because tips don't count as part of a restaurant's revenues, but higher menu prices do. So if a venue increases prices to pay staff more, its revenues go up accordingly, and it must pay more sales tax.William Michael Lynn, professor of food and beverage management at Cornell University and author of The Psychology of Tipping, says the problem of going tip-free is that customers struggle to get their heads around the maths."Higher menu prices make dining out seem more expensive because people do not adequately take into account that they are no longer tipping," he says. "It leads to lower demand."Image source, Amanda CohenImage caption, Amanda Cohen says customer are pleased when the realise they don't have to tipIn New York, vegetarian restaurant Dirt Candy was one of the very first to ban tipping back in 2015. "I wanted to make it more equal for everybody," says chef and owner Amanda Cohen, who now pays her staff about $30 an hour.She says that many customers "are pleasantly surprised when they realise they don't have to tip 20% on top".Cassidy Van der Kamp is a filmmaker whose YouTube documentary Tipless was inspired by her own experience of working in a restaurant in Oakland, California which went tip-free.While some other servers left, Van der Kamp, who was originally paid about $10 an hour plus tips, decided to stay and earned $21 per hour after the change."I had stability for the first time as I knew what I was earning… and I didn't need to look at a low tip and think what did I do wrong?"'Tipping fatigue'While Van der Kamp liked the move, Lynn says that a huge challenge of moving to a gratuity-free system is that it can be difficult to attract and retain waiting staff who like getting tips.However, given the growth of what has been called "tipping fatigue" – people being increasingly annoyed at having to pay high tips – will more restaurants stop the practice?"Despite tip-fatigue, I do not think tipping is going to be eliminated on widescale anytime soon because the economic disadvantages of eliminating tipping outweigh the advantages," says Lynn.Back at Nightshade Noodle Bar, Miller doesn't regret her decision. "The clearest measure is that staff stay."Turnover in this industry is brutal, and we have people who have been here since we made the change. It has proven to be highly valued by my guests and team."

schema.headline: Why some US restaurants are banning tips

title: Briton Bradley Townsend killed fighting for Russia in Ukraine
description: Image source, OTHERImage caption, Bradley Townsend left South Yorkshire in April, reportedly telling his family he was going to RomaniaByTom AireyAndr
body: Image source, OTHERImage caption, Bradley Townsend left South Yorkshire in April, reportedly telling his family he was going to RomaniaByTom AireyAndrew Jackson and Corinne WheatleyYorkshireA British national has been killed in Ukraine while fighting for Russia.Bradley Townsend is said to have died following an attack by a remote-controlled FPV drone in Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region. His death, on 10 June, is believed to be the first of a British citizen fighting for Russia in the conflict.The 33-year-old left his home in Barnsley, South Yorkshire, earlier this year after telling his family he was going to Romania, according to the Yorkshire Post, external.The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was aware of reports a British national had died in Ukraine, adding it was in contact with his family.The news emerged as Andy Burnham arrived in Kyiv for his first foreign trip as UK prime minister.The visit coincides with the 35th anniversary of the country's independence from the Soviet Union.The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Andy Burnham has promised to keep up the pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats", on his first official visit to Ukraine as UK prime ministerIn a video shared online on 4 April, Townsend featured alongside Ben Stimson and Aiden Minnis - who were given Russian citizenship for fighting in the occupied Donbas region.In the video, uploaded to a Russian recruitment account, Townsend described himself as "a normal working-class lad from Yorkshire".Filmed by Stimson with Minnis interviewing, Townsend discussed the implications of his decision to leave the UK and fight for Russia during the video.He said: "I came with the idea that I probably won't be able to go home, definitely get persecuted if I went back."He later added: "I'm not here for a suicide mission, but I understand that's what can happen."Stimson, from Oldham, and Minnis, from Wiltshire, are believed to be the first British nationals fighting for Russian president Vladimir Putin since he ordered the full scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Stimson was previously jailed in the UK in 2015 for joining pro-Russian separatists in the east of Ukraine.Image source, GMPImage caption, Ben Stimson was jailed in the UK before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine after travelling to join a pro-Russian group in the regionMinnis announced the death of Townsend, using the Yorkshireman's call sign of Badger, in a social media post.The FCDO said it advised against all travel to Russia and "our ability to provide consular support in these circumstances is severely limited".Its foreign travel advice for Ukraine warns travelling to Ukraine to fight or to assist others engaged in the war may amount to offences under UK legislation."You could be prosecuted on your return to the UK," it adds.A number of British nationals have been killed during the war.However, they have all been fighting for Ukraine, following Russia's attacks on the country since 2022.Townsend is thought to be the second man from Yorkshire to die during the war, with 18-year-old James Wilton, from Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, killed in 2024 after he volunteered to fight for Ukraine. title: Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints as he visits Kyiv
description: Burnham vows support for Ukraine despite 'outrageous threats' from RussiaFigure caption, Is UK's Storm Shadow missile a game changer for Ukraine?ByHen
body: Burnham vows support for Ukraine despite 'outrageous threats' from RussiaFigure caption, Is UK's Storm Shadow missile a game changer for Ukraine?ByHenry Moore and Imogen JamesAndy Burnham has promised to keep up the pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats", on his first official visit to Ukraine as UK prime minister.Burnham met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.He said the coalition was "doing everything we can" while urging the US Congress to "ratchet up" economic pressure on Russia.The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically.Burnham said allies were doing "everything we can" to "dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks" of air defences to protect Ukraine."This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia, the moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war," Burnham said, praising the "strength" of the Ukrainian people. "Ukraine has been Europe's protector, not a drain on our security but the front line in keeping Europe safe."It comes after Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace.He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them."Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"He said the issue of missile interceptors would be the main topic at the coalition of the willing meeting. Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Burnham accepts an award from Volodymyr Zelensky on behalf of the British people recognising the UK's support for UkraineImage source, ReutersImage caption, Burnham chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing" in KyivBurnham has been reaffirming the UK's backing for Kyiv in the wake of escalating Russian strikes on Ukraine in recent weeks - including one on a shopping centre on Friday that killed at least 16 people. In a joint statement after the meeting, Burnham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgent priority".They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the "shadow fleet".The Coalition of the Willing is a partnership of 34 countries including Ukraine. Members met on Monday in either Kyiv or by video conference, with a release stating "leaders once again reaffirmed their commitment to support Ukraine's independence".It came as the European Union said it had released €6.1bn (£5.2bn) in military aid for Ukraine to boost its air defences. The finance is part of a wider €90bn loan from the EU to Ukraine.The UK and Ukraine have also announced a new military technology partnership, external giving British experts access to Kyiv's Avengers AI Labs database. Downing Street says Ukraine has used sensors and cameras to capture data across the battlefield and it can be used to train AI models "to solve key national security challenges" faced by both countries.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Burnham lays flowers at the graves of Ukrainian soldiers during a Monday serviceOn Monday morning the prime minister laid flowers at the graves of Ukrainian soldiers during a service at the National Military Memorial Cemetery.He accepted an award from Zelensky on behalf of the British people recognising the UK's support for Ukraine during an independence day event outside the St Sofia cathedral in Kyiv. In a speech, Burnham compared Ukraine's resistance to Russia to the UK's fight with Nazi Germany, saying: "My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st."In a statement issued ahead of the visit, the prime minister said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes."I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."Moscow earlier warned of "consequences" over the use of British drones by Ukraine in its recent ramping up of strikes on Russian infrastructure.Kyiv has stepped up long-range attacks on Moscow and other Russian regions, targeting oil refineries and warehouses of the country's largest online retailer, Wildberries.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesThe government is allowing UK defence company MBDA to declassify information on its components for the Scalp missile, as Ukraine and France aim to establish assembly lines in Ukraine.Scalp missiles and its UK-produced version, the Storm Shadow, have already been provided to Kyiv by both Britain and France and used to hit military targets inside Russia.What are the Storm Shadow missiles Ukraine has fired into Russia?Ukraine hopes it can also be given more Patriot interceptor missiles, with Zelensky again asking for more of the weapon, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles. Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriots, but its stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.The Russian embassy in the UK has accused Britain of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis", saying "the deeper its involvement in the conflict... the higher the price it will pay".In response, Burnham said last week: "We are not fair-weather friends, we will be there in Ukraine's hour of need and that won't change."Asked on Tuesday about the Russian threat, Burnham maintained the UK was "providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself and that's been the British position all the way through this conflict, by previous prime ministers - it remains the case with me".The visit comes as Russia confirmed its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, had left his post in London in recent weeks.The Kremlin is yet to put forward a replacement but Russia's embassy to the UK told the BBC it did not reflect an intention to downgrade diplomatic relations between the two nations.Deadly exchanges between Russia and Ukraine continued overnight, with two children killed and seven injured when Ukrainian drone debris hit a private children's centre in Russia, local authorities say.A warehouse belonging to online retailer Ozon was also set on fire, two days after Ukraine said it would target the company for selling dual use items that could be used by the military.It was at the third night in the row that Ozon's warehouses had been targeted, with the company confirming on Saturday that a logistics centre in the Samara region had been hit and a warehouse in Orenburg on Sunday.Three people were also killed in a Russian attack on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

title: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByMark PoyntingClimate reporterThe world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from huma
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByMark PoyntingClimate reporterThe world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from human-caused climate change and the growing El Niño weather phenomenon.The average surface temperature of the planet's seas outside the polar regions hit 21.1C (70F) on Saturday, according to figures from the European Copernicus climate change service.That edges past the 21.09C recorded on three separate days in March 2024, and is far above average for the time of year.Warmer oceans can have wide-reaching consequences, including supercharging extreme weather, raising sea levels and harming marine life."This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress," said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus."El Niño is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming," she added.The data is based on sea temperatures 10m (32ft 10in) below the surface, using measurements from buoys, ships and satellites, which are combined to produce a global estimate.While the margin of record is currently very small and any global estimate comes with uncertainties, scientists say its timing is particularly notable. Average worldwide sea temperatures tend to reach their yearly peak in March or April, which corresponds to the end of summer in the southern hemisphere - and not in August.The southern hemisphere contains more of the planet's ocean surface than the northern hemisphere and so exerts a bigger influence on average sea temperatures.What is especially concerning to scientists is that the oceans are already so hot when the natural El Niño weather phenomenon is still some way off its expected peak.El Niño brings unusually warm waters to the surface of the eastern and central tropical Pacific Ocean. Warmer waters across such a large area means that global average temperatures typically spike too.El Niño is expected to keep strengthening until Christmas time, with scientists warning that it is on course to be the strongest in centuries.This could see ocean temperatures climb yet further."The fact that we are already breaking records is an early indicator of how strong the El Niño is becoming," said Dr Jeremy Grist, senior research fellow at the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton. "All things being equal we might expect the ocean temperature record to be broken again in March [or] April 2027," he added. The waters far away from El Niño's Pacific hunting ground are also extremely warm, including around the UK and Europe.The western English Channel has seen almost continuous marine heatwave conditions for more than three years, peaking at 7C above normal in July, according to Prof Tim Smyth, director of science at Plymouth Marine Laboratory.“This is unprecedented,” he added.Scientists say such widespread warmth around the planet is a clear sign of the growing effect that human-caused climate change is having on the world's seas. The oceans take up more than 90% of the excess heat trapped by humanity's greenhouse gas emissions, mainly from burning fossil fuels. "The latest Copernicus data reinforce the troubling upward trend in ocean temperatures,” said Smyth.Warmer seas help to fuel more extreme weather. They can provide storms with extra moisture and energy, and can intensify heatwaves on land in some coastal regions by reducing the cooling effect of sea breezes.Warmer water also takes up more space, raising sea levels and bringing a greater risk of coastal flooding - while intense ocean heat can be devastating for sea habitats, such as coral reefs.The increasing frequency of marine heatwaves is already "putting increasing pressure on marine ecosystems and the communities that depend on them", Burgess said.Figure caption, Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather?Get in touchWhat questions or concerns do you have about El Niño?

schema.headline: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows

title: Charity? Acting? The Cotswolds? What will Harry and Meghan's UK life look like?
description: Speaking in June last year to British businesswoman and podcaster Emma Grede, Meghan talked about her Netflix lifestyle series With Love, Meghan, and
body: Speaking in June last year to British businesswoman and podcaster Emma Grede, Meghan talked about her Netflix lifestyle series With Love, Meghan, and hinted at a return to acting when asked if she missed that side to her life."Sometimes," Meghan replied. "Being back on set with With Love, Meghan was great because I realised how much I miss my crew. I love being around a crew."But Variety's chief correspondent Marlow Stern says when it comes to deliberations over a potential acting role for Meghan, "a lot of it has to do with scheduling, to be honest"."They're maybe also negotiating the size of the role and how many days she'll shoot, and also compensation for it. Both sides often play the media to try and push things along, and we could be seeing that."For Harry, the focus once back in the UK will be on the charity work and patronages he has kept hold of while living thousands of miles away.He has now completed his final charity engagements in the US before flying back to the UK in the coming days.In Washington DC, he met military veterans and their families and visited America's main hospital for injured servicemen and women, Walter Reed National Military Medical Centre.At Arlington National Cemetery, he visited the final resting place of many service personal killed in Iraq and Afghanistan wars where he himself served on two operational tours.At the grave of Sergeant Michael Verardo, who died last year from complications related to injuries sustained in Afghanistan in 2010, he met Verardo's widow Sarah - who now supports other military families - and their nine-year-old daughter, Elizabeth.The couple will keep their multi-million dollar home in Montecito, about a two-hour drive north of Los Angeles. Meghan's mother, Doria Ragland, who has been heavily involved in helping to care for her grandchildren, will remain living in California.The family is expected to return to the US regularly as well as use the holiday home they have bought near Melides in Portugal. It is close to a property bought by Princess Eugenie and her husband Jack Brooksbank who have remained close to the Sussexes during the royal fallout.How involved Harry, Meghan, Archie and Lilibet will be with the wider royal family has not yet been decided.Over the next few months, several significant royal engagements are in the diary that would involve most senior royals - Remembrance Sunday at the Cenotaph, the Princess of Wales' Carol Service at Westminster Abbey and then Christmas at Sandringham.Will there be invitations extended to the Sussex family?Trust remains an issue. There is caution, a degree of wariness and even hostility in some quarters of the Royal Household. These decisions are very much a work in progress.Harry and Meghan's team has described the move to the UK as being for "an extended period of time".It is not necessarily a long-term move but may be a chance for the family to experience life in the UK, allowing the children to get to know their grandfather, the King, while they are young enough to not have their education disrupted.Much of what happens in the months ahead will be a test - of Harry and Meghan's liking for life in the UK, of public reaction to them and of the royal family's ability to continue with their duties alongside the distractions the Sussex family may bring.Additional reporting by James Govan.

schema.headline: Charity? Acting? The Cotswolds? What will Harry and Meghan's UK life look like?

title: US Open 2026 qualifying results: Heather Watson among British winners in New York
description: Britain's Heather Watson battled back from a set down against Claire Liu to keep alive her hopes of securing a first US Open main-draw appearance in f
body: Britain's Heather Watson battled back from a set down against Claire Liu to keep alive her hopes of securing a first US Open main-draw appearance in five years.The 34-year-old Watson beat sixth seed Liu 4-6 6-2 6-4 in the first round of qualifying in New York.Watson almost let a double-break lead slip in the final set but held firm to set up a meeting with Spain's Angela Fita Boluda.Toby Samuel, Jacob Fearnley, Billy Harris and Harry Wendelken all progressed in men's qualifying.Samuel, seeking to reach the US Open main draw for the first time, fought back against Italy's Francesco Maestrelli to win 6-7 (2-7) 6-3 6-1 and set up a meeting with fellow Briton Harris.Harris progressed with a 6-1 6-3 win against Peru's Gonzalo Bueno.Fearnley claimed a 7-6 (7-3) 6-3 victory over Spain's Roberto Carballes Baena to set up a meeting with Frenchman Luka Pavlovic.Wendelken will meet Swiss player Remy Bertola after overcoming Italy's Stefano Travaglia 6-4 3-6 6-3.However, Liam Broady lost 7-6 (7-4) 6-3 against Italy's Marco Cecchinato, while Felix Gill was beaten by Italian Francesco Passaro 7-6 (7-3) 6-2.Players must come through three rounds of qualifying to reach the singles main draw, which gets under way on Sunday.In the mixed doubles competition, Britons Henry Patten and Lloyd Glasspool will both seek to beat some of the sport's biggest stars after coming through two qualifying matches on Monday.The US Open mixed doubles was controversially revamped last year to include singles stars in a bid to attract more attention to the format.Under the new format, the top six pairs with the best combined singles rankings received direct entry into the main draw, with another eight receiving wildcards.The tournament now takes place over three days in the week before the main draw began, and features a shorter scoring system with only four games required to win a set in matches before the final, no 'advantage' scoring and 10-point match tie-breaks instead of a third set throughout.Both Patten and Glasspool had to come through qualifying with their respective partners on Monday.Patten, a two-time winner of the men's doubles competition at Wimbledon, and Czech team-mate Katerina Siniakova defeated Americans Peyton Stearns and Christian Harrison in straight sets in their second qualifying match.Next, Patten and Siniakova - the respective men's and women's world number ones in doubles - will take on 24-time major winner Novak Djokovic and top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka in the first round of the main draw.After defeating El Salvador's Marcelo Arevalo and France's Kristina Mladenovic, Glasspool and New Zealand's Erin Routliffe will face 23-time Grand Slam singles champion Serena Williams and seven-time major winner Carlos Alcaraz.Alcaraz will be playing his first match in four months after recovering from a wrist injury, while Williams is making her return to the sport after a four-year absence.

title: Keely Hodgkinson withdraws from Zurich Diamond League as body "not quite ready"
description: Keely Hodgkinson has withdrawn from the women's 800 metres at Thursday's Diamond League meeting in Zurich because her "body is not quite ready".Olympi
body: Keely Hodgkinson has withdrawn from the women's 800 metres at Thursday's Diamond League meeting in Zurich because her "body is not quite ready".Olympic champion Hodgkinson had been set to go head-to-head with Switzerland's Audrey Werro, who beat the Briton to gold at the European Championships in Birmingham earlier this month."Unfortunately the body isn't quite ready to race again after the European Championships," Hodgkinson said in a statement."We've made the decision to skip this race and get ready for the next one. Sad to miss it, hopefully see you next year!"The race will feature world 400m hurdles champion Femke Broeders-Bol, who has stepped up to the 800m this season, and Hodgkinson's training partner Georgia Hunter-Bell, who won 800m gold at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow last month.World 800m champion Lilian Odira of Kenya, who beat Hodgkinson and Hunter-Bell to gold in Tokyo last year, has pulled out of the race after suffering from illness and weakness since the Commonwealth Games.While Diamond League organisers said they were looking forward to Hodgkinson's "highly anticipated race against Audrey Werro", they "fully respect" the Briton's decision and "hope to see her back in Zurich in the future".After suffering hamstring and knee injuries over the past few years, Hodgkinson skipped the Commonwealth Games to prioritise the European Championships amid a busy summer schedule."I signed myself up for Zurich because I knew everyone was in it but me. I want to be in with the best and I think that's going to bring out the best in me," Hodgkinson said in Birmingham earlier this month.Before winning 800m gold at the London Diamond League on 18 July, Hodgkinson said she was feeling "definitely a lot better than I was".Thursday's meet in Zurich is the penultimate Diamond League event of the season, with the final to take place in Brussels over two days on Friday 4 and Saturday 5 September.

schema.headline: Keely Hodgkinson withdraws from Zurich Diamond League as body "not quite ready"

title: Brydon Carse: Michael Vaughan says England need punishment to 'send a shiver'
description: A punishment to "send a shiver down the whole team" may be needed after Brydon Carse became the latest England cricketer involved in a drinking contro
body: A punishment to "send a shiver down the whole team" may be needed after Brydon Carse became the latest England cricketer involved in a drinking controversy, according to Michael Vaughan.Pace bowler Carse was briefly placed under arrest on a night out with his Durham team-mates in Derby at the weekend.The incident is being investigated by the Cricket Regulator and, as a result, Carse has been removed from the England squad for the second Test against Pakistan at Lord's on Thursday."Someone is going to have to get a punishment that sends a shiver down the whole England cricket team and right down through the programme, so that everyone knows that if you misbehave or bring any kind of bad reputation on to this team, you know what's going to come," former England captain Vaughan told BBC Radio 5 Live."It's the only punishment that will really hurt players."In October, England white-ball captain Harry Brook was punched by a bouncer outside a nightclub in Wellington, New Zealand, with team-mates Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue also present.During the Ashes tour of Australia, opener Ben Duckett was filmed apparently drunk on England's holiday in Noosa.And in June, former Test captain Ben Stokes and pace bowler Gus Atkinson broke a team curfew and were present when a member of England's security staff was punched by a Saracens rugby player in a London nightclub.In this latest incident, Carse was with Durham team-mates Stokes and Matthew Potts, all of whom are under England central contracts. In Stokes' case, the England deal remains in place despite his international retirement in June.It makes a total of eight contracted players who have been involved in or present for late-night incidents in the past year – more than a quarter of the 30 men on England deals.In this latest occurrence, footage shared on social media on Sunday showed Carse in handcuffs, surrounded by police officers.And, although Vaughan said it is an "awful look for the England team once again", he would "feel" for Carse if he is made an example of following the other events of the past year."I hope Carse is getting good support around him," said Vaughan. "He is a character who can be a little bit loose and if you give him a bit of rope he'll take a huge amount of it. He needs people around him who are giving him better advice."I would feel for Carse if he is the one who takes the rap for what has happened over the past nine months, but somewhere, somehow, something has to be done to set a precedent that they won't stand for that behaviour any more."On Monday, the England and Wales Cricket Board confirmed that the Regulator was investigating and, as a result, 31-year-old Carse had been removed from the squad for the second Test, with his place going to Sonny Baker.Soon after that, Derbyshire Police said a man in his 30s was arrested on Saturday night, only to be de-arrested a short time later."A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night, 22 August," said a police statement."However the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards having agreed to leave the area."This new controversy comes only one game into Joe Root's second spell as Test captain.Before his first game back in charge, an innings defeat of Pakistan at Headingley, Root called on his players to be "good role models and good human beings".Now, Root will speak to the media on Tuesday to address the fallout from the Carse incident."Joe Root will be absolutely fuming with this," said Vaughan. "He will have been hoping to arrive at Lord's to talk about cricket and his team."Now he will have to answer all these questions about discipline, curfews and drinking culture."Everything we thought has been brushed under the carpet and moved to one side, we are pretty much back to square one."Former England spinner Phil Tufnell agreed with Vaughan that a substantial punishment is the only way to ensure players fall in line.Tufnell, who had multiple brushes with authority during his international career, said: "If you want to stop this, the only way you stop it is say: 'You're not playing for five games.'"I was made to stand in the corner during my England career, was told: 'You're not available for selection.' It will soon stop. It would be cleared up in a jiffy."Carse was in the England squad for the first Test but not selected in the final XI. It is unlikely he would have been in the team for the second Test at Lord's, unless one of England's four frontline seamers from Headingley suffered a fitness issue.Since Carse made his Test debut in October 2024, no England bowler has more Test wickets than his 58. He was the only member of England's attack to play all five matches in the Ashes series in Australia.However, he was unavailable at the beginning of the home summer because of an injury, and being removed from the squad for the second Test could push him further down the pecking order."Carse is 31 and coming to the autumn of his career," said Tufnell. "You need to keep yourself fit."You want to be bowling these long spells for England and making a name for yourself."It's probably best not to be doing that [going out so late]. Some of the best in the business have tried and failed at doing that."

schema.headline: Brydon Carse: Michael Vaughan says England need punishment to 'send a shiver'

title: Organised crime arrests as police investigate A66 crash that killed seven
description: Twelve people have been arrested as part of the investigation into the A66 crash that killed seven people, including two police officers.Nine men and
body: Twelve people have been arrested as part of the investigation into the A66 crash that killed seven people, including two police officers.Nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61, have been arrested across Teesside on suspicion of a range of offences including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.In the early hours of Saturday, a Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by police travelled the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough and crashed into an oncoming police car - two PCs and all five Passat occupants died.Cleveland Police said it was investigating "serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident".PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and 17-year-old Cole Robert Worthy.Earlier, Cleveland Police released more details of its investigation into the lead-up to the crash and information about the 12 people it had arrested.The force said:It received several reports of two vehicles "being driven dangerously" on Saturday morningThe first vehicle, believed to be a Volvo XC60, was seen "ramming properties" in the Middlesbrough areaThe second vehicle, a Passat, is believed to have been associated with this activityBoth vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technologyThe Volvo has been recovered in MiddlesbroughFour of the five people in the Passat had previous convictionsAssistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said the investigation had been "fast moving and complex".He said: "The events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect."We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident and to bring all those responsible to justice."An online fundraiser set up for the officers' families by the Cleveland Police Federation has raised more than £500,000.PC Blades' wife said he "gave his life in the line of duty, protecting and serving others with courage, dedication and selflessness".Before joining Cleveland Police, PC Blades worked as an English teacher at Carmel College in Darlington.The college said: "Many within our community will remember Matty as an intelligent, kind and approachable teacher, a valued colleague and someone who gave generously of himself to the young people in his care."The family of PC Clough described the former soldier as "our hero".They said he "jumped into action whenever needed" and was "willing to help anyone for any reason".The family statement added that he "proudly fought for his country to make the world a better place".Flags at Cleveland Police headquarters are flying at half-mast and Redcar and Cleveland Council has opened a book of condolence at its offices on Ridley Street in Redcar.Floral tributes can also be left at the memorial garden at the force's headquarters in Hemlington or any Cleveland Police station, the council said.Tributes for the five young men have also been shared on social media, with many of their friends saying they were "heartbroken" and "lost for words". Balloon releases have been announced in their memory.Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Tees on BBC Sounds.

schema.headline: Organised crime arrests as police investigate A66 crash that killed seven

title: China's humanoid robots are stealing the show, but a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC visits factories in China with robot workersByLaura BickerChina correspondentReporting fromBeijing, Hangzhou and Chengdu"I
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC visits factories in China with robot workersByLaura BickerChina correspondentReporting fromBeijing, Hangzhou and Chengdu"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spending his spare time in factories that are switching to automation. That way he knows what to prioritise when teaching his class about artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.In front of him, around 30 college students are studying code. One of them is typing furiously as his eyes dart from the screen to the robot: "The idea is it will grab that cylindrical piece and move it over there."A line of industrial robots are waiting to be programmed, and in another part of the classroom, students are trying to develop robotic medical instruments. As he guides them, Chen declares: "If you are not needed by the world of AI and robotics, then you'll definitely be among those eliminated".For the people in this room, this is a step - or rather a leap - towards a future that China is meticulously building: Xi Jinping's $20bn (£14.7bn) plan to put his country at the forefront of innovation and in direct competition with the US.The evidence is all around them. They are in the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of several huge, purpose-built vocational schools that want to churn out the next generation of tech-savvy engineers. The campus sits on the outskirts of Hangzhou, a former imperial capital whose futuristic skyline is just the first hint of its role as a global tech hub.Across the country, there are more than two million robots working in China's factories - which is more than anywhere else - and they are continuing to scale up at extraordinary speed.Image caption, Students learning robotics at the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of many new vocational schoolsIt is a commitment that will surely change the world, much like the last time the Chinese economy underwent a massive transformation. It is already shipping its robots across the globe: more than half of the world's industrial robots are now made in China.What is less clear is the impact of such sweeping automation in a country that sits at the heart of global manufacturing, trade and innovation. What does this mean for China's human workforce, for instance? And how would we be able to truly measure the cost of this transformation in a regime that controls information so tightly?The future of China's workers is uncertain in the industrial revolution the world has been watching: gleaming solar grids, peak hours made noiseless by electric vehicles, machines that run faster than Usain Bolt. Over the weekend, China hosted the second edition of the World Humanoid Games where robots boxed, sprinted and marched.What is fuelling this spectacle is another, less visible revolution happening inside factories and classrooms.The BBC has visited industrial sites where we have been shown robots that do not look human, or dance or leap on stage but weld, paint, lift, assemble and work around the clock without a break or benefits. Some are designed to build more robots. We have also been inside academies where China is training the people who will work alongside its robotic workforce.This is a front-row seat to what Xi calls China's "new productive forces" - and how they could reshape the country.Image caption, More than two millions robots work alongside people in China's factories On a factory floor in the southern city of Chengdu, the old and and the new are working side by side.An assembly line of around 30 middle-aged men and women is screwing, drilling and polishing CRP Technology's signature product: a robotic arm which performs various industrial tasks. Also in the room are four young engineers crowded around a console, trying to crack the code for a prototype, a new robot that they hope will help build other robots.One of them, 31-year-old Pang Kai, who is part of the research and development team, pushes the sleek skeleton across the room. Because China's future workforce is not quite ready to strut out. For now, it can only do simple repetitive movements, such as scan a QR code."Maybe in another half year, it can do another task," Pang says, smiling wistfully. It's a long road and the team are celebrating every small win.CRP Technology, which employs around 300 people, has been building robot arms for nine years. Each arm can be tailored to a factory's needs to help build cars, electronics or wind turbines. The firm says a single arm can be programmed to perform more than 90% of repetitive tasks.The engineers also wonder if, one day, they can replace the company's workforce. "We want our new robot to be like human beings. We hope it can think by itself," says Pang. "We need these kinds of robots because maybe in 10 years, we won't have enough workers in China."Image caption, A team of young engineers is trying to build a robot that can build other robots  A shrinking population and an ageing workforce is another reason Beijing is in a hurry to revolutionise its factories. By 2035, more than a third of China's population will be over 60, according to official estimates. The country will also lose nearly 60 million people in the next decade - almost equivalent to the population of France - according to some estimates.The hope is that increased automation will fill this looming gap in the workforce before it starts to affect an already sluggish economy. But the speed of the transition is key. Around 120 million people still work in the manufacturing sector. If China moves too quickly, job losses could follow dealing a catastrophic blow to millions who depend on factory wages."In theory, machines can work 24 hours a day, which is certainly an advantage compared with human workers. But machines also require maintenance. Every day we need time for that, and each month the production line also requires inspection and repair," says Cao Li, vice-president of EV maker Leapmotors.Increasingly popular in Europe and the UK, the company's budget-friendly, tech-focused cars come together at the Hangzhou factory with robots aiding the process at every step. At the end of the assembly line, more humans emerge.The company has more than 25,000 workers and hundreds of them make the final checks as the sparkling new vehicles roll past. Will there be a day when they are no longer needed?"It's entirely possible," Cao says. "And it may come relatively quickly. In workshops, including stamping, welding, and painting, we've basically achieved 100% automation."Image caption, Machines are part of every step in making Leapmotors' EVsChina has the edge over the US due to its enormous manufacturing base. Motors, batteries, electronics, gears, sensors - everything needed to build the body of a robot is all at hand."China also has an idea. It has a plan. They know where they want to be in five years. They plan at a top level, but they break it down to the regions, to the municipalities," says Dr Susanne Bieller, General Secretary of the International Federation of Robotics."If you want to build a robot in Shenzhen - there's an entire ecosystem. It takes you less than one hour to source the components you need to make a robot. In Europe it can take you up to a week."However, she acknowledges that while China is good at building the body, the US is still leading at building the "brain", which includes developing the AI to programme robots. And yet Chinese firms, from DeepSeek to Moonshot, have been unveiling new AI models that they say can compete with top US firms.Driven by an "open-source" approach, where AI start-ups share their code, Chinese innovation has been able to catch up faster than expected, despite US export controls over critical advanced chips. Analysts now believe that the next leg of this race will be determined not by who has the best language model, but who can put this intelligence into millions of machines.Image caption, Chinese innovation is powering the country's factories faster than expected   And that is why China is also investing in producing a generation of students learning to imagine what could come next.At the Hangzhou Technician Institute, for example, children can start from the age of 15. And the scale of what is being taught can feel staggering. There is an entire building dedicated to engines and aeronautics, and a restricted floor for students who will work to keep China at the forefront of processing rare earths - another crucial commodity in the battle with Washington.Some see this as a solution to China's stubbornly high youth unemployment rate, with one in five struggling to find a job. "Our students are in demand and can even be pre-booked by companies. They don't need to worry about employment at all, and we hold competitions as part of their training," Chen, the young teacher, says."It's better to find your position within the technological wave. In the process of progress, structural changes are bound to occur, and these structural changes are exactly where students' future employment opportunities lie."But China still faces serious economic challenges, from a property crisis that continues to drag on to huge local government debt and persistently low consumption. It is unclear if and how the revolution Beijing is touting will fix these, and it is hard to gauge how those whose jobs are threatened feel about the change that is coming. Will robots create prosperity for them, or simply take many of their jobs?"My students ask me what will happen in the future," Chen says. "I say I don't know. Technology is changing so fast. But we can't just stand still and sleep here. We have to move forward to see what we are capable of doing."

schema.headline: China's humanoid robots are stealing the show, but a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
